title: Antonelli reveals race number he will use to defend title in 2027
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has revealed what race number he will use to defend his Formula 1 drivers' title in 2027, having become World Champion in the Mexico City Grand Prix.

The Italian became the youngest driver to clinch the F1 title at the age of just 20 after finishing third during Sunday's 71-lap race at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez.

Antonelli took nine wins this year on his way to the title during his sophomore season, and only failed to reach the podium in three races.

Now that Antonelli has clinched the title, the Mercedes driver has a first-time decision to make – what race number he will use to defend his crown in 2027?

Since 2014, drivers have been able to pick their own race numbers, with the number 1 reserved only for the current champion to use.

Previously, Lewis Hamilton continued to use number 44 when winning his six titles for Mercedes, while Max Verstappen and more recently Lando Norris this season decided to use the number 1 after their title-winning campaigns.

Antonelli currently uses 12, the same number used by his idol Ayrton Senna when the Brazilian claimed the first of three titles with McLaren in 1988.

When asked post-race in Mexico what Antonelli would do for 2027, the new champion admitted the number 12 held even more special significance now.

"I think I'll stay with number 12," he said. "I'll stay with number 12 because, obviously, it's a very special number for me.

"But also it's a way for me to stay grounded, to stay humble, and I feel like by keeping number 12 it allows me to have a new point where to start and build on everything again and try to improve.

"And also, to be honest, I'm very superstitious, and number 1 has never been a good number for me. Whenever I put it, it went extremely badly. So one more reason to stay with number 12. But, yeah, I will stay with number 12."

title: Hirakawa assesses 'dream' F1 debut in Mexico City
excerpt:
Ryo Hirakawa's Formula 1 debut "was my dream" after the Japanese driver finished the Mexico City Grand Prix, eventually being promoted into the points.

Hirakawa was a late call-up to the Haas team, replacing Esteban Ocon at the American outfit on Saturday morning, but having already taken part in Free Practice 1 as a designated 'rookie' driver.

With another hour of practice under his belt, the 32-year-old eventually qualified P19 before starting his maiden Grand Prix from a spot higher on the grid after a penalty for Liam Lawson.

Hirakawa circulated in the midfield battle for much of the 71-lap race at Autodromo Hermanos Rodríguez on Sunday, eventually finishing P13 on the road, with seeing the chequered flag his ultimate goal.

But things became even better post-race, as Hirakawa joined an exclusive club of drivers to score points on their F1 debuts after time penalties for Oscar Piastri and the two Alpines of Franco Colapinto and Pierre Gasly promoted him to P10.

"Was a lot of things to do, especially the start and lap one, it was not easy," said Hirakawa before being promoted into the points.

"Especially here going to Turn 1 is so long you think about a lot of braking points, the cars side by side, in front, behind. So I think the start I took too much margin because I really wanted to finish the race because I want to learn. But it is what it is.

"After that I was trying to learn from the others what they are doing. Maybe the first stint was really tough, we didn't have the pace but I learnt a lot. After the Safety Car with the C5 [tyre], then I had more confidence and passed two cars. I'm happy to finish like that."

Haas are yet to confirm their driver line-up for this coming weekend in Brazil, with Hirakawa originally scheduled to compete for Toyota in the World Endurance Championship, where the title remains up for grabs.

Looking to the future, Hirakawa admitted he just had to savour the moment in Mexico for what might prove to be his only F1 start.

"I think I just need to taste this moment. I'm really happy, today was my dream," he said. "Just enjoy this moment and see what we can do."

excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli became Formula 1's youngest ever champion with another assured drive, this time in the Mexico City Grand Prix, but as the Italian celebrated making history, many of his rivals – namely Italian squad Ferrari – had very little to smile about. Lawrence Barretto selects his winners and losers from the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez.

Winner: Kimi Antonelli

Antonelli's pass on Charles Leclerc late in the Mexico City Grand Prix to take a podium perfectly encapsulated his bold, brave pursuit of a maiden world title in his second season.

title: Antonelli's incredible journey to his maiden F1 title
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has made history by clinching his maiden World Championship, the Mercedes racer becoming the youngest-ever driver to take the crown after embarking on a stunning sophomore campaign. F1.com charts the journey of his triumphant 2026 season, from an initial setback through to his incredible run of victories…

Round 1, Australia – Bouncing back from an early crash

The season did not necessarily start in perfect fashion for Antonelli, with the youngster suffering a heavy crash in Free Practice 3 at the Australian Grand Prix. He quickly bounced back, however, by claiming P2 on the grid, which he converted into the same position come race day, helping Mercedes to secure a 1-2 finish alongside team mate George Russell.

Round 2, China – Converting first pole into maiden win

One week later in Shanghai, the tables turned at Mercedes. While Russell took another win in the Sprint, it was Antonelli who scored his maiden pole position – making him F1’s youngest-ever polesitter – before storming to his debut victory on Sunday.

Round 3, Japan – Becoming the youngest-ever championship leader

Antonelli’s impressive run of form continued at the Japanese Grand Prix, with another pole position and win resulting in the Italian climbing to the top of the drivers’ standings – a feat that saw him become the youngest driver to ever head the championship at 19 years, seven months and four days old.

Round 4, Miami – Making history with another win

Next time out in Miami, Antonelli dropped backwards in the Sprint, picking up a penalty for track limits en route to a P6 finish. Once again, however, the youngster recovered by seizing pole position and resisting pressure from a chasing Lando Norris to take another victory, making him the first driver in history to convert their first three poles into wins.

Round 5, Canada – Another win amid heartbreak for Russell

The Mercedes intra-team battle turned up a notch in Montreal, with Russell beating Antonelli after a fierce fight for the lead during the Sprint. Russell went on to secure pole for the Grand Prix, where the team mates resumed their thrilling scrap on track – but the duel came to an early end when Russell was forced to retire due to a power unit issue, resulting in Antonelli’s championship lead increasing to 43 points.

The records Antonelli has broken on his way to maiden title

Round 6, Monaco – Triumphing around the streets of Monte Carlo

Winning the Monaco Grand Prix is a feat that most drivers dream of achieving, and Antonelli boosted his chances of reaching the milestone by adding another pole position to his tally during an exciting Qualifying. The title leader kept his cool to win an eventful race, while penalties for Russell saw the British driver leave the event with no points.

Round 7, Barcelona – Title lead cut down after dramatic retirement

After climbing up to P2 during the latter stages of the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix – following a close battle with Russell – Antonelli’s race came to a sudden end when he was forced to pull off track with a mechanical issue. The Italian admitted that his first retirement of the campaign had left him feeling “a bit empty”.

Round 8, Austria – Another boost for Russell in championship fight

The momentum again looked to be with Russell as F1 returned to Austria, with the Briton converting pole position into a victory. Antonelli had to settle for P3 behind the Red Bull of Max Verstappen, meaning that his championship lead now stood at 40 points.

Round 9, Great Britain – Sprint victory followed by a challenging race

Antonelli got back to winning ways at Silverstone by triumphing in the Sprint for the first time, having overtaken polesitter Lewis Hamilton on Lap 8. Race day was not quite so straightforward, however, with the youngster dropping backwards through the field due to a left front wheel shield failure. A penalty for track limits ultimately left him in P16 – a result that reduced his advantage in the standings down further to 25 points.

Round 10, Belgium – Return to the top step as title lead increases

Two weeks later in Belgium, Antonelli bounced back with his sixth pole of the season and a commanding victory on race day. Russell, meanwhile, found himself out of the running early on following Lap 1 contact with Hamilton, meaning that Antonelli now held a 45-point lead in the title fight.

Round 11, Hungary – Extending his lead despite challenges

After his pole and victory at Spa, Hungary proved to be a more challenging weekend for Antonelli and Mercedes – the Italian having to settle for P4 in Qualifying before being demoted to seventh on the grid for a yellow flag infringement. A different strategy and late-race Virtual Safety Car (when some rivals pitted again) brought him into podium contention, though, and he came away with P3 and an extended title lead.

'Unbelievable' - The F1 grid praise new champion Antonelli

Round 12, Netherlands – Strong starts “save” Antonelli’s race

When the Zandvoort Sprint weekend began, Russell appeared to have the upper hand in the Mercedes intra-team battle – the Briton taking P1 on Saturday, and Antonelli settling for fourth. However, in the Grand Prix itself, Antonelli launched past his team mate from the second row and then challenged Norris for the lead, before finishing runner-up to the McLaren man via a tough final stint on hard tyres.

Round 13, Italy – A comeback drive for the ages

Antonelli headed into his home Grand Prix weekend knowing that he would be starting from the back of the grid due to an engine-related penalty. What followed was an epic recovery drive that will no doubt go down as one of his finest performances in the sport. Starting from 19th, he was up to 14th by the end of the first lap and 12th after the second lap, before charging his way through the points-paying positions – eventually passing team mate Russell for a memorable win.

Round 14, Spain – Capitalising on Norris’ VSC misfortune

Antonelli was second-best to Norris in Qualifying at the all-new Madring, and it looked as though the McLaren driver would convert his pole into victory on race day with a strong start. However, an early Virtual Safety Car – coming out just at the wrong time for Norris – handed the lead to Antonelli, who controlled the remainder of the encounter to make it back-to-back wins.

Round 15, Azerbaijan – A tricky weekend on Baku’s streets

Antonelli faced a couple of major challenges when the Azerbaijan Grand Prix got underway, having lost valuable track time in practice due to technical problems and then crashing in the Q1 phase of Qualifying. While he recovered from 16th to fifth, Russell dominated proceedings, and Antonelli admitted afterwards that it represented “the worst weekend of the season for me”.

Round 16, Bahrain in Malaysia – Taking a huge step towards the title

The tables would turn once more next time out at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, which tested the drivers with rough tarmac and mixed weather conditions. As a dramatic wet/dry race drew to a close, Russell dramatically retired with an engine failure, giving Antonelli a clear run to second place – and another massive boost in terms of the championship situation.

Round 17, Singapore – Making his dream a mathematical possibility

Although Antonelli reported struggling with Mercedes' "very difficult" upgraded car during the early stages of the Singapore Grand Prix weekend, it didn't seem to show too much in his results. He finished fourth in the Sprint before improving to the podium on race day, and with Russell settling for a hard-fought P9, the Italian set himself up for a potential title win at the next round.

Antonelli's dad reflects on son's 'important' title triumph

Round 18, United States – Dominant victory edges him even closer

Arriving at the Circuit of The Americas with a 102-point lead over his team mate, Antonelli needed three things to go his way: one more race win, Russell to finish ninth or below, and Hamilton to place outside of the top four. He delivered on his side, converting what Toto Wolff described as a "miracle lap" in Qualifying to a supreme victory. Everything from his launch to tyre management and strategy was close to flawless, but both of his nearest rivals in the standings wound up just one position higher than he required, delaying what now seemed inevitable for one more week.

Round 19, Mexico City – Third on track, first in the history books

He had executed a champion's drive in Austin, so all that separated Antonelli from his record-breaking maiden title was a P9 finish in Mexico City. For the racer who had only missed out on the podium at three Grands Prix, that didn't sound like too big an ask. While he unsurprisingly felt "more tense than usual" before lining up in the P4 grid slot, he delivered the kind of level-headed performance he's grown into this season and snatched third place from Charles Leclerc. The subsequent podium celebration won't be forgotten any time soon, with the Italian hoisted onto the shoulders of two of the sport's most successful racers on the podium in Verstappen and Hamilton.

title: Bonnington names Antonelli’s top three races in title year
excerpt:
Pete Bonnington has selected his favourite three races that set Kimi Antonelli on the path towards becoming the 2026 World Champion, praising the Italian for his “mind-blowing” achievement.

Head of Race Engineering Bonnington – or ‘Bono’ – is no stranger to title success, having acted as Lewis Hamilton’s race engineer during his incredibly fruitful stint at Mercedes that saw him triumph six times between 2014 and 2020.

Once Hamilton departed the team for the 2025 season, Bonnington continued in his role for rookie Antonelli, guiding him through a challenging campaign before the now 20-year-old began to thrive under the new-for-2026 regulations.

After nine Grand Prix victories, Antonelli finished third at the Mexico City Grand Prix to secure the Drivers’ Championship, becoming the youngest to do so in the history of F1.

Asked which highlights stand out from the record-breaking season, Bonnington told F1 TV: “I think three stand out, and I think people will know what those three races are.

“For me, Monaco was just super special. It’s one of those races where if you can prove that to the rest of the grid, I think your peers respect you even more, and the way that he did it was just unbelievable.

“And then the Monza race… just wow. I remember turning around thinking, ‘oh, this is what the back of the grid looks like’, and then off we went. There was no stopping him.

“And then last weekend in Austin, that was a champion’s drive. It was the one-stop versus the two-stop. There’s the mental pressure in the car thinking, ‘I’m going to get caught, I’m going to get overtaken’, but no, he just kept his head down. He kept putting the lap times in and came out on top.

“Three drives of the year that really sealed that performance, but to be fair, other ones like Silverstone… without the failure, that would’ve been a really good result. Barcelona, we were looking good as well, so it’s that repeated performance that’s consistent. He can drive across a range of tracks, be it overheating, tyre warm-up, whatever.”

Bonnington is admired for his calm radio messages during races, but he and Antonelli have also garnered a reputation for pranking each other, with their off-track hijinks regularly shared across social media.

While it may not align with the high-stakes world of F1, the experienced race engineer insisted that having a more light-hearted relationship has been crucial to the Italian’s ability to remain focused and bounce back when he needs to.

“You can pick up a load of management books that will tell you any successful organisation has an element of fun in it, but he just does it naturally,” he explained. “It’s the way that he feels most comfortable, and it’s the way that he gets everyone else to feel comfortable.

“By having that element to the way that we work, it just sort of breaks down barriers so we can have open and honest conversations because we know at the end of the day we can still have a laugh and a joke. It’s a real big part.”

Elaborating on what Antonelli’s achievement means to him, he said: “Mind-blowing, I think is the word. It’s just been such an amazing journey with him. He’s really matured over this year and wow, he’s just grown into the World Champion that he is.

“It’s been a real fun year – the way that he’s brought that element into the team. He is the consummate professional and just such a talent.”

title: The records Antonelli has broken on his way to maiden title
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has made history by becoming F1’s youngest-ever World Champion, the Italian sealing his maiden title in only his sophomore season – but that’s not the only record he has broken during his run to the crown.

F1.com has rounded up the historic feats achieved by Antonelli across his stunning 2026 campaign…

Youngest polesitter

Two rounds into the championship, Antonelli secured pole position for the first time at the Chinese Grand Prix. While he had previously taken the P1 slot in Sprint Qualifying during F1’s visit to Miami in 2025, this marked his maiden Grand Prix pole.

As such, the Mercedes driver became the sport’s youngest-ever polesitter at 19 years, six months and 18 days old – beating previous record holder Sebastian Vettel by some margin, the German having been 21 when he took his debut pole position at the 2008 Italian Grand Prix.

Youngest winner from pole position

George Russell had emerged triumphant in the Sprint hours before his team mate claimed that historic pole position in Shanghai – but it was Antonelli’s turn to stand on the top step come Sunday.

The then-teenager put in an assured performance to convert his P1 grid slot into his debut win, making him the youngest driver to ever win from pole. Max Verstappen continues to hold the record for the sport’s youngest-ever winner, the Dutchman first tasting victory when he was 18 years old.

'Unbelievable' - The F1 grid praise new champion Antonelli

Youngest driver to lead the championship

Just two weeks after that success in China, Antonelli’s impressive run of form continued when he seized his second win at the Japanese Grand Prix – a feat that also saw him climb to the top of the drivers’ standings.

This also resulted in him breaking yet another record by becoming the youngest-ever leader of the World Championship at 19 years, seven months and four days old – beating the statistic previously held by Lewis Hamilton when he headed the table aged 22 in 2007.

First driver to win from first three pole positions

Having converted pole into a win both in China and Japan, the streak extended to three times in a row as Antonelli put in another strong drive at Round 4 in Miami.

As well as building his championship lead, this latest achievement saw Antonelli become the only driver in history to win from their first three pole positions.

Youngest winner of the Monaco Grand Prix

Antonelli ultimately scored five victories in a row across the opening stages of the season, adding two more consecutive triumphs to his name after his success in Miami.

Perhaps most notably, the fifth of these wins occurred at the Monaco Grand Prix. The Italian kept his composure around the tight and twisty streets of Monte Carlo to once again stand on the top step of the podium, making him the youngest-ever winner of the famed event.

Youngest driver to achieve a Grand Slam

A Grand Slam – when a driver starts from pole position, sets the fastest lap, leads the race from start to finish and achieves victory in one weekend – is an illustrious feat in F1. As things stand, only 29 drivers across the sport’s long history have one to their name.

Antonelli joined that list in Monaco, making him the youngest driver ever to earn this accolade.

First Italian home winner in 60 years

The Italian Grand Prix marked Antonelli’s seventh win of the season and perhaps one of his greatest moments so far, the Mercedes racer having risen from the back of the grid to the top step of the podium in front of his local crowd.

And as if that wasn’t special enough, the event was made all the sweeter for the driver from Bologna as he became the first Italian to triumph in their home race since Ludovico Scarfiotti in 1966.

First Italian World Champion in 73 years

Following on from that memorable victory at Monza, Antonelli has given Italy even more to cheer about by ending the country’s 73-year wait for their next World Champion.

The youngster is only the third Italian to take the crown; Giuseppe ‘Nino’ Farina was F1’s inaugural champion in 1950, before Alberto Ascari clinched back-to-back titles in 1952 and 1953.

'People were doubters' - Wolff on Antonelli's title glory

Youngest World Champion

As mentioned earlier, one of the most talked-about statistics that Antonelli has now claimed is that of becoming Formula 1’s youngest-ever World Champion.

The record was previously held by Sebastian Vettel, who was 23 years, four months and 11 days old when he clinched his first title with Red Bull in 2010.

First driver born in the 2000s to become World Champion

The past five seasons have seen a driver born in the 1990s win the World Championship – that being Max Verstappen (the first from that decade to achieve the feat in 2021) and Lando Norris.

Antonelli, however, is the maiden title-winner born during the 2000s – 2006 to be exact, the same year in which fellow active champion Fernando Alonso took the crown for a second time.

title: Russell details ‘frustrating’ opening lap issue in Mexico
excerpt:
George Russell endured another “frustrating” issue with his Mercedes on the opening lap of the Mexico City Grand Prix that hampered his chance to win, with the Briton ultimately bringing home eight points in P6.

A competitive Qualifying saw Russell miss out on pole position by just 0.009s to Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton, but his quick start at lights out was cancelled out by a deployment problem that saw him lose multiple places.

He ended up in a battle for fifth with Isack Hadjar and tapped the rear of the Red Bull, sending his rival into a spin and subsequently receiving a 10-second time penalty for the collision.

Russell then managed to hold off McLaren’s Lando Norris before peeling into the pits, where his longer stop meant he lost P5 in the race and P2 in the Drivers’ Championship, his team mate Kimi Antonelli securing the latter with his third-place finish.

“Firstly, congratulations to Kimi on a thoroughly deserved championship,” Russell reflected. “He has done a fantastic job this season and can be incredibly proud of what he has achieved.

“Unfortunately, it was a very disappointing race on my side. I made a good start and was in a strong position, but then we suffered an issue which caused me to not have full deployment down the straight.

“That cost us a lot of positions and ultimately took us out of contention for a strong result. It’s frustrating to have the race compromised by something outside of my control but that is racing.

“We will reset after this weekend and look to come back stronger in Brazil. We still have a Constructors’ Championship to win and my full focus is on helping the team achieve that.”

Russell has borne the brunt of Mercedes’ reliability struggles this season – in Belgium, for example, he suffered poor deployment that similarly saw him caught up in contact with another driver.

The bad luck that has impacted his results at times left Team Principal Toto Wolff to take responsibility after the Mexico City Grand Prix, especially as a race win could’ve softened the blow of his team mate being crowned World Champion.

“I saw George after the race on the scales and obviously he is distraught about the situation,” Wolff told written media after the race. “It was a great show of sportsmanship to go and see Kimi. I have known George for such a long time.

“He is going through a hard time. For a racing driver this is a catastrophic moment and maybe today the race was a little bit a picture of his season, you know, this was a race for him to win.

“We had the pace in the car, and we let him down on the first straight. The energy delivery is not what we thought it should be. And so, I'm very much with him at the moment – I've been in situations where it’s very difficult to cope.”

title: ‘It's a matter of respect’ – Vasseur on Hamilton/Leclerc clash
excerpt:
Ferrari Team Principal Fred Vasseur couldn't hide his frustration after an intra-team battle on the opening lap of the Mexico City Grand Prix proved costly in a race that held such promise.

On the face of it P2 and P4 was a decent result in the context of the highly competitive battle among the top four teams. However, this was a race that the Maranello team should have won – and it was lost after Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc raced each other too hard on the first lap, opening the door for Max Verstappen and Red Bull to take the victory.

The frustration was that the hardest part of the job had already been done. Not only did polesitter Hamilton hang onto top spot on the drag to Turn 1, from his third spot Leclerc was able to jump front row man George Russell and slot into second.

It was at the tight Turn 4 that the red cars both ran wide as they disputed the same piece of road and, while Leclerc cut across the grass to take the lead, Hamilton rejoined the track, lost momentum, and was passed by Verstappen.

It was obvious to all that Leclerc had gained an advantage and had to cede the place, but matters were complicated by the Red Bull being in between the Ferraris.

He opted to stick it out and build an advantage before he earned the inevitable penalty – five seconds when the stewards had the option for 10 – and he subsequently lost the lead to Verstappen when he took it at his stop.

After the red flag and resumption Hamilton got up to second, but he could do nothing about the RB22 up ahead on a day when managing temperatures made it hard to follow. Having locked up the restart Leclerc was perhaps fortunate to hang on to P4.

After the flag Vasseur did not hide his frustrations when speaking to the media. For a few brief seconds Ferrari had run one-two at a track where passing is hard, and between them the drivers had seemingly scored a massive own goal. Leclerc blamed the track layout, but Vasseur saw a bigger picture.

Hamilton reflects on costly Ferrari intra-team battle in Mexico

“The layout of the track for sure is not helping,” he said. “Because if you have a look, the last couple of years we had this kind of issue. But it can't be an excuse at all.

“Honestly, I'm a bit frustrated, because I think we did a proper step forward in terms of performance the last couple of events, and we were one-two at Turn 4. I don't remember the last overtaking in Mexico, perhaps at the end of the seventies.

“And when you are one-two at Turn 4, you don't imagine that you don't win the race. It's a lot of frustration for me, but I'm not the most important. I think it's a lot of frustration for the 2,000 people working for the project – and this I will need time to digest.”

Asked if there had been a pre-race discussion about first lap protocol, he said: “I think we can discuss ages for this, but it's not a matter to discuss before if you are on the right-hand side, if you are on the left-hand side. My only discussion, it's a matter of respect.”

Vasseur reiterated his opinion on respect when asked about the drivers putting their own interests above that of the team.

“I think this is typically what respect means,” he said. “They are not working for themselves. They are working for a group. They are working for a lot of sponsors. They are working for the 2,000 people of the company. The guys, when we had to push for the upgrades, they were working night and day – and we have to keep this in mind.”

Leclerc said he wanted better direction from the pit wall about giving back the place or not, and Vasseur admitted that it wasn’t easy to make a call.

“It was not very clear,” he said. “We had discussion with the race control. But you have to act before Turn 11. Turn 11, you have five seconds delay between the video and the reality, it meant that you are already in Turn 11."

What he did indicate was that Leclerc could, or perhaps should, have made his own decision.

“The regulation is clear that you have to give back the position in this case, before Turn 11. And we agreed before the race that they have to do it by themselves.”

Vasseur, however, didn’t want to be drawn on Hamilton’s suggestion that the team had “big problems,” heard on team radio after the red flag.

“Let me discuss with them," the Ferrari boss added. "I don't want to interpret what they said in the radio.”

Leclerc concedes he 'deserved penalty' over Hamilton clash

So were there any positives to be drawn on a weekend when the SF-26 took pole and showed such good pace?

“The positive is that my frustration is coming from there,” said Vasseur. “We did a good step forward in terms of pure performance. Now it's the third or fourth race in a row that we are scoring more points than our competitors.

“We did a pole position. The pace was good enough to do one-two, and for sure it's more frustrating when you are in this situation than if you do a P15 and P16 in quali. For sure the frustration is there.

“But now the advantage is that we have another one in four days. We will discuss tonight, we will fix it tomorrow, and then we focus on Sao Paulo."

As Vasseur made clear, Ferrari does at least have a car capable of winning.

“Honestly, we are all in the ballpark,” he said. “If you have a look on all the sessions, one time it's Charles, one time it's Lewis, one time it's Max, one time it's Norris yesterday. It means that we are all there. It's much more linked to the track layout and engine sensitivity than just the package or the concept.

“But yeah, I think we are there with the others, and it will be another fight in Sao Paulo next week. It's good for the F1, good for the championship, this kind of situation when you have six, seven or eight guys who can win the race on the first season of the regulations.”

George Russell has issued a statement after his title defeat to Kimi Antonelli.

George Russell has released his first public comments since Kimi Antonelli claimed the Formula 1 drivers' title in Mexico City.

After the Italian finished third to become the youngest F1 champion, Russell quickly left the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez without talking to the media, something which earned Mercedes a €5,000 fine.

Russell had finished sixth after incurring a 10-second time penalty for a collision on the opening lap with Isack Hadjar after starting on the front-row - but where a deployment issue on the run to Turn 1 had dropped him down the order.

title: Liam Lawson lands 'done everything' praise as F1 future uncertainty grows
excerpt:
Racing Bulls CEO Peter Bayer has acknowledged that Liam Lawson has "done everything" he can to prove himself within the team.

Lawson has enjoyed a successful campaign this year and has been a regular finisher inside the points, with 83 to his name after the Mexico City Grand Prix.

The New Zealander is on course to end the campaign ninth in the drivers' championship, the first position outside the drivers from the leading teams.

However, he has not yet secured a drive on the 2027 F1 grid and is believed to be facing competition from Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov.

While Lawson has impressed, Bayer insisted that Racing Bulls' core goal is to assess fresh talent when it becomes available.

"He has certainly done everything to prove himself," Bayer told ORF. "That's also the general consensus in the paddock.

"As a team that plays a leading role in developing new Formula 1 talent, it's our job to continually bring new drivers into the series.

"We've already helped a total of 22 drivers make it to Formula 1, including Sebastian Vettel and Max Verstappen.

"That's why I also say that the decision will ultimately rest with Alan. He'll make the right choice for the team."

Bayer issues praise to challenger Tsolov

Tsolov is currently fighting for the Formula 2 title and sits seven points down on leader Rafael Camara with two rounds to go.

The Bulgarian made his F1 weekend debut last weekend in Mexico, taking part in FP1 as part of the mandatory rookie outings teams must provide.

Tsolov ended the session in 12th, drawing praise from Bayer.

"Nikola's stint on Friday was really great. It was his first time in this car, and he integrated perfectly into the team.

"As for the decision regarding next year's driver lineup, that decision rests with Alan.

"He'll make a decision and announce it when he thinks the time is right."

title: Toyota issues incredibly emotional letter after ‘unforgettable’ Hirakawa F1 debut
excerpt:
Ryo, congratulations on your F1 debut! And most of all, thank you. From the bottom of my heart. Ever since Toyota withdrew from F1 in 2009, there has been a feeling I have carried with me.

I believe every racing driver dreams of one day driving the fastest car in the world. I wanted to find a way to make that dream come true for our drivers. I wanted to see a Toyota driver race in F1 again.

That was a dream I had quietly held in my heart for 17 years. Through our partnership with Haas, we gradually created opportunities for our drivers to take on the challenge of F1, through testing and FP1 sessions.

And now, 17 years after 2009, that day has finally come. One of Toyota’s drivers has raced in a Formula 1 Grand Prix. And I could not be happier that it was Ryo Hirakawa.

When I last met Ryo, it was after he had faced a difficult outcome in his pursuit of a full-time race seat for the following season. At that time, Ryo promised me that he would never give up.

Drivers are reaching F1 at an increasingly young age. And I felt truly sorry that Ryo had to go through so many difficulties along the way.

I told him, "When you have to make a choice, choose the path that makes you happy. Choose what you really want to do." Even so, Ryo never stopped preparing.

He kept himself in the best possible condition, ready to deliver his very best whenever an opportunity might come along, even though nobody knew when that opportunity would arrive, or whether it would ever come at all.

He kept going without any guarantee that his efforts would be rewarded. That is why I am so happy to see him make his F1 debut.

After driving in FP1 on Friday, Ryo was suddenly called up the following morning to drive in FP3 and qualifying on Saturday, and then the race on Sunday. With very little time to prepare, he showed the pace to fight for a place in Q2, and in the race, he kept pushing right to the end.

The final result may not have been what he had hoped for. But seeing Ryo take on the world’s highest level of motorsport with such confidence and determination made me incredibly proud. When I saw Ryo line up on the F1 grid, I felt that one of my own dreams had finally come true, too.

Ryo, thank you for making my dream come true. I also want to express my heartfelt thanks to Gene Haas, Ayao Komatsu, and every engineer, mechanic and member of the TGR Haas F1 Team.

This day would not have been possible without your trust in Ryo, your support, and the tremendous effort of every single person in the team. It takes so many people working together to make one driver’s dream of racing in F1 come true.

To each and every one of you, thank you. Truly. My heartfelt thanks also go to Ryo’s family, who have supported him throughout his journey, to the fans who never stopped cheering for him, and to everyone else who has supported him along the way.

Ryo’s drive has brought dreams and inspiration to so many children. In endurance racing, Ryo has already reached the very top of the world. Now, I hope he can take the next steps in Formula racing, too. First, scoring points. Then, standing on the podium. I want all of us to cheer him on, together with the fans, one step at a time.

And one day, I hope to see a Japanese driver standing on the top step of an F1 podium. Nobody knows when the next opportunity will come. But after everything Ryo has endured, all the patience he has shown, and all the hard work he has put in while continuing to believe in his dream, I believe he will give us another reason to dream.

Gene, Ayao, and everyone at TGR Haas F1 Team, Let’s continue creating opportunities for our drivers to chase their dreams. Building cars and going racing are never things we can do alone. It is about people connecting, becoming friends and teammates, and chasing dreams together.

I want to keep racing forward with all of you, as one team. Ryo, thank you for giving us such an unforgettable moment. And thank you for making my dream come true, too!

title: Lewis Hamilton scolds Charles Leclerc 'do or die' mentality after latest clash
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has scolded Charles Leclerc for his approach to wheel-to-wheel racing, suggesting his team-mate needs a mentality shift going forward.

The Ferrari duo were involved in an opening lap scrap for the lead of the race, with both running into Turn 4.

Leclerc was subsequently given a five-second time penalty for gaining an advantage off the track, which eventually handed the lead to Max Verstappen, who slipped ahead of Hamilton after the opening lap skirmish.

Hamilton stated after the race that he was "really pissed" with the situation, while Ferrari team boss Fred Vasseur accused both drivers of lacking respect.

It is not the first time this year Hamilton has felt aggrieved with his team-mate, as they also had an opening lap tussle at Monza that resulted in the seven-time champion losing several places.

Hamilton asserted that Leclerc's approach to racing is nothing new.

"Before I joined this team, when I was at Mercedes, I watched and witnessed the back-and-forth between Charles and Carlos several races," Hamilton told media including RacingNews365.

"They were battling so much that the person ahead just pulled away, and they had the pace to actually win."

[Article continues below]

Hamilton points to 'kamikaze' avoidance at Silverstone

Hamilton started the race from pole position, having achieved his first with Ferrari on Saturday in Mexico.

The incident between the duo severely hindered Ferrari's chances of a third win in 2026.

Hamilton called on his team-mate to look at his approach from Silverstone earlier this year, when he avoided a "kamikaze" move to strip Leclerc of a race win.

"It is one thing when that's happening in fourth and fifth, as opposed to first and second, and you lose the win," he said.

title: Kimi Antonelli crowned, Ferrari implode as Mexico delivers title chaos - Winners & losers from the Mexico City GP
excerpt:
It was a never-to-be-forgotten weekend in Mexico City as the stories just kept on coming. We dissect and bring you the winners and losers from a frantic few days.

Formula 1 has a new youngest world Champion after Kimi Antonelli sealed the drivers' title in Mexico City with a measured third-place finish behind another consummate performance from race-winner Max Verstappen.

Meanwhile, Ferrari self-destructed, sparking ructions between Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc; George Russell suffered a miserable afternoon, and Haas axed Esteban Ocon mid-weekend.

Here are your full winners and losers from a captivating few days in Mexico City.

© XPB Images

Winner - Kimi Antonelli

Kimi Antonelli did not need to win the Mexico City Grand Prix to make history; ninth position would have been good enough.

At the flag, Antonelli finished a fine third behind two of the greatest of all time, Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton.

At 20 years and 68 days old, the Mercedes driver became the youngest champion in F1 history, surpassing the previous record, held by Sebastian Vettel, by an astonishing three years. He is also the first Italian to lift the drivers' title since Alberto Ascari in 1953.

While Ferrari imploded around him and his own team-mate, George Russell, endured a nightmare, Antonelli simply it clean and let the points come to him to mark his place in the annuls of the sport.

© Red Bull Content Pool

Winner - Max Verstappen

Max Verstappen took full advantage of Ferrari's self-inflicted chaos, inheriting the lead after Hamilton and Charles Leclerc tangled on the opening lap, which saw Leclerc pick up a track-cutting penalty.

Despite a second restart from 'pole', after a horrifying front-left suspension failure on his Cadillac at 200mph sent Valtteri Bottas hurtling into a barrier, Verstappen was unflappable on this occasion en route to his third win of the campaign.

The result was all the more impressive because he started fifth after a one-place grid penalty for a second-practice clash with Liam Lawson. Verstappen also set the fastest lap, rubbing salt into Ferrari's wounds.

© XPBimages

Winner - Ryo Hirakawa

Parachuted into the Haas seat on Saturday after Esteban Ocon's sudden axing, Ryo Hirakawa became F1's oldest race debutant since Andre Lotterer in 2014.

The 32-year-old needed no time to settle in, and when post-race penalties dropped rivals down the order, his Haas was elevated to 10th, handing him a championship point on his first grand prix appearance.

© XPBimages

Loser - Ferrari

Ferrari arrived with a genuine shot at victory, with its smaller turbocharger seemingly giving it an edge at altitude.

Instead, Hamilton, who had ended a three-year drought by securing pole position, and third-on-the-grid Leclerc squabbled for position on the opening lap.

Leclerc was eventually handed a five-second penalty for leaving the track and gaining an advantage after failing to give the place back, much to Hamilton's annoyance over the radio and post-race.

Serving the penalty at a pit stop, Red Bull immediately also brought in Verstappen, who had maintained a small gap to Leclerc, allowing the four-time F1 champion to leapfrog the Monégasque for the lead, a position he maintained to the flag.

Although Hamilton salvaged second, a maiden win that looked there for the taking, slipped away through indiscipline.

© XPB Images

Loser - George Russell

George Russell qualified on the front row, only for an electrical deployment problem off the line and down to Turn 1 to wreck his race before it had barely started.

Fighting back through the field, he then clattered into the rear of Isack Hadjar's Red Bull at Turn 6, spinning his rival and earning a 10-second penalty.

A slow pit stop then cost him fifth place to Lando Norris, leaving him to settle for a lowly sixth. Mercedes was also fined 5,000 euros after Russell skipped his mandatory post-race media duties to the understandable devastation at seeing team-mate Antonelli be crowned champion.

© XPBimages

Loser - Esteban Ocon

Esteban Ocon's weekend ended before the race had even started, with the Frenchman dropped by Haas midway through the event.

In practice on Friday, Ocon was involved in a tense dispute with his race engineer over tyre running plans. On Saturday morning, it was announced he was dropped, with Haas making clear it was not for health reasons.

Ocon later issued a statement confirming internal disagreements had occurred while denying rumours of any physical altercation as the reason for his exit.

Haas has not detailed its disciplinary reasoning, and it remains unclear whether Ocon will be back in the car for the team's home-stretch races.

Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff admitted Russell was “distraught” over the situation as he opted to skip his post-race media duties.

Rosberg, who endured title glory and agony during his career, acknowledged it's a dark time for Russell.

“It is scary because he doesn't know, 'is this going to have to continue like this now into the whole of next year, or am I going be able to get back?'” Rosberg told Sky F1.

“It's a scary moment.”

[Article continues below]

Rosberg issues advice to Russell

Rosberg suffered title defeat to Lewis Hamilton in 2014 and 2015 before finally getting his hands on the trophy in his final year in the sport.

Offering some advice to Russell after he missed out on the title, Rosberg said: “Get away from it and forget, first of all.

“Get away, do something different, get away from the sport, forget, and then start preparing for the new season.

“Remember your great moments, he's had so many. He is one of the greatest drivers out there, I don't really know what happened this year.

“So remember, and prepare the hell out of it. George is very good at preparing.

“He's very good at that. He's exceptional at preparing himself. He's really, really brilliant.

“But the problem is, Kimi is also pretty good, apparently.”

title: Aston Martin 'fail moment of truth' after basic Mexico challenge 'underestimated'
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso believes Aston Martin and Honda "underestimated" their "moment of truth" test in Mexico City after power unit failures wrecked his weekend.

Despite believing his car could have challenged for a strong Q2 spot at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodríguez, Alonso was told to stop after just one flying lap in qualifying, with a water pressure issue.

New parts were fitted for the race, but both Alonso and team-mate Lance Stroll retired after just five laps with what the team called "abnormal pressure levels in the PU systems."

A key challenge of the weekend was dealing with the altitude of Mexico City, which is 2,285m above sea level, and where air density is around 20% lower than at sea level.

This meant the turbos had to work harder to provide the demanded power by drivers, but with the removal of the MGU-H from the 2026 power units, a crucial tool in eliminating turbo lag was also taken away, to add to the challenge.

Reflecting after a promising round of practice sessions, including FP1 where Alonso's seventh best was Aston Martin's best result in any session all season, the two-time champion felt the car had failed its ultimate "moment of truth" test and that the altitude challenge had been "underestimated."

"We did as much as we could [in trying to protect the power unit], but Mexico always provides very big challenges for the power units, and even with that, it seems that it was not enough, so we had to retire the car," Alonso told media, including RacingNews365.

"Two short laps in qualifying, and the race is very frustrating because the three free practices were fine - we did a lot of laps in FP1, FP2, and FP2.

"And then when we got to the moment of truth in qualifying and the race, we didn't manage to do enough laps.

"But this is part of the process of learning, and hopefully we can learn hard lessons and learn things from [this weekend]."

Turning to his retirement, Alonso then added that he knew it was a "shared problem" with Stroll when the sister car retired, before adding that he felt "the challenge with the altitude was probably underestimated by the power unit."

Check out RacingNews365's Driver Ratings from the 2026 F1 Mexico City Grand Prix

The Mexico City Grand Prix saw Kimi Antonelli clinch his maiden world championship after crossing the line in third place.

The Italian once again drove a mature race to third on the road, which was more than enough to seal the deal.

There was drama at Ferrari on the opening lap, while Max Verstappen managed to take his third victory of the season as he benefitted from the drama at the Scuderia. But who gets our strong ratings, and who failed to impress?

See the Mexico City GP driver ratings below!

The top five

Max Verstappen - 9

Verstappen started fifth after a grid penalty but made it count, running the only medium-tyre strategy among the front-runners. The Red Bull driver profited from opening-lap chaos between the Ferraris and nailed his pit-stop timing to come through for a commanding victory at altitude, his third of the season.

Lewis Hamilton - 9

Hamilton topped qualifying and backed it up with a composed drive to second. Although he was inconvenienced by the opening lap tussle with his team-mate, the Ferrari driver kept Verstappen honest for large stretches and ensured Maranello's weekend ended with a notable result.

Kimi Antonelli - 8.5

Antonelli produced the brilliant pass during the race, moving ahead of Charles Leclerc into Turn 1 at the restart to claim third. The result was enough to make the Mercedes driver Formula 1's youngest-ever champion, a fitting way to wrap up the title. Given the pressure of the occasion, the composure he showed in that fight for the podium made the achievement all the more remarkable.

Ryo Hirakawa - 8.5

Hirakawa impressed on his Haas debut weekend, showing respectable pace during qualifying following his late call-up. In the race, he kept himself out of trouble and ended up being promoted into 10th after the stewards' post-race deliberations. A points finish on debut is a result few could have predicted, and it offered an encouraging first glimpse of what the Japanese driver could bring to the American outfit in the seasons ahead.

Liam Lawson - 8.5

Lawson was disqualified from qualifying and forced to start from the pit lane after unapproved parc fermé changes. The Racing Bulls driver still fought back through the field to finish in the points, a recovery drive that stood out on a chaotic afternoon as he continues to plead his case to be retained for 2027.

The bottom five

Franco Colapinto - 5.5

Colapinto had looked set for a solid haul of points before the stewards intervened. The Alpine driver was stripped of his finish for failing to slow sufficiently under yellow flags, turning a promising run into a blank scoresheet. It was a frustrating end to what had otherwise been one of his more encouraging weekends behind the wheel this season.

Nico Hulkenberg - 5

Hulkenberg's prospects for the race looked promising after he qualified inside the points but his hopes of a strong result were dashed when he clumsly hit into the back of Oliver Bearman. As a result, he was handed a 10-second time penalty.

Pierre Gasly - 5

Like Colapinto, Gasly also lost a points finish to the stewards after failing to respect yellow-flag conditions. The Alpine driver's afternoon ended in similar fashion to his teammate's, with a promising run wiped from the results. It compounded a difficult day for the French squad, who had looked set for a rare double points haul before the penalties struck.

Lance Stroll - 4.5

Stroll pulled off the circuit and retired on Lap 7, just moments after teammate Fernando Alonso brought the sister Aston Martin into the pits. The cause of the Canadian's early exit was not immediately disclosed by the team, capping a forgettable weekend for the Silverstone-based outfit as they left Mexico City without anything tangible to show for their efforts.

title: Lando Norris and Charles Leclerc reflect on karting roots as FIA marks 70th anniversary
excerpt:
Where would today's F1 stars be without their karting roots?

Karting celebrates its 70th anniversary this week, with the FIA using the build-up to the 2026 Mondokart.com FIA Karting World Championship to reflect on a discipline that has become the foundation of modern motor sport.

The sport traces its roots to California, where Art Ingles and Lou Borelli built the first kart by fitting a 2.5 horsepower lawnmower engine to a steel tube chassis. What began as a way of getting around paddocks at car races grew into a recreational pastime in American car parks by the late 1950s, before spreading to Europe and prompting the FIA to establish the International Karting Commission in 1962.

The first Karting World Championship followed in 1964, and the sport has since produced some of motor racing's biggest names.

François Goldstein won five world titles between 1969 and 1975, a record later broken by Mike Wilson's six championships in the 1980s. Alain Prost became the first of many karting graduates to go on and win the Formula 1 drivers' title.

This weekend's World Championship for OK and Junior categories takes place at La Conca in southern Italy, with nearly 200 drivers chasing the title won by reigning F1 champion Lando Norris in 2014.

The FIA launched its Global Karting Plan in 2024 to make the sport more affordable and accessible, centred on an Arrive and Drive format in which all competitors race identical, loaned equipment.

The approach cuts competition costs by two-thirds compared with standard international events and has already spawned dedicated championships in Asia-Pacific, South America and Europe.

FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem said the anniversary was a chance to acknowledge karting's role in shaping the sport's biggest stars.

"As we celebrate the 70th anniversary of karting, we recognise a legacy that has helped shape generations of racing talent and produced many of the legends who have gone on to achieve success at the highest levels of our sport," said Ben Sulayem.

"Through the FIA Global Karting Plan, we are helping to secure the next 70 years of karting by making it more affordable, accessible and inclusive, so that talented young drivers from every corner of the world have the opportunity to compete and fulfil their potential."

[Article continues below]

Norris - 'I miss the karting days'

Norris, the 2014 FIA Karting KF champion, said karting remains the essential grounding for any aspiring F1 driver.

"[Karting is where you] learn how to drive; you learn how to feel what is right, what is wrong, all those things that set you up to be an understanding driver and how to drive quickly, so it's very important," said Norris.

"It's probably key if you want to get to Formula 1 nowadays is to start early and in karting. It’s a lot of fun.

"I think everyone enjoys the karting days a lot and misses them and just the ease and socialness- it’s just a lot more chilled than it is in proper racing now in cars, but they were good days. I miss the karting days.”

Ferrari's Charles Leclerc, who won the FIA Karting Academy Trophy in 2011, said the bonds formed on the karting circuit have carried through into F1.

“[Karting] is where you learn all the basics, which is to start working with the team, start thinking about the set-up, overtaking, the way you've got to approach a race and, eventually, also how to deal with pressure when it matters most in qualifying – and a few incidents!," said Leclerc.

“It's cool as well to see, when I look at the grid today, that many of us were fighting in karting 15 or 20 years ago. It's very special to find all of us now in Formula One and fighting for much bigger things.

"The passion is still the same, and the motivation to win is still the same. These were the best days. There wasn't much marketing or media, just racing, and I think that's what we enjoyed most. These were great times."

title: Kimi Antonelli 'couldn’t see' Mexico track on final lap: 'I lost two seconds'
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has stated he was struggling to see the track in the final laps of the Mexico City Grand Prix as he got closer to clinching the F1 title.

Antonelli entered the race needing only ninth on the road to become the youngest champion in the sport's history.

After staying out of trouble on the opening lap, Antonelli stayed in contention for a top-three finish and consolidated third after making a late-race overtake on Charles Leclerc.

As he closed out the race, Antonelli revealed that he was losing considerable time as he could no longer keep his emotions under control.

"Already the lap before, I lost probably two seconds because I was already crying, basically," Antonelli told media including RacingNews365.

"I couldn't see clearly ahead. I could see two Ferraris somehow with the tears.

"It was very special. A lot of memories went through my mind in that moment, all the memories since karting all the way to here.

"It was a very special final lap, and definitely, then when I crossed the line, I let it all out because it was just achieving one of my biggest dreams. It was very special."

Antonelli highlights 'critical' Leclerc overtake

Antonelli was gunning for an even higher result than third after making his pit stop as he extended his opening stint, before a red flag neutralised the race.

As he chased the podium finish, Antonelli described his overtake on Leclerc as "critical" as he dealt with his systems overheating.

"We had a strong pace, especially in that first stint, when we went for 40-plus laps on the soft, and we were still very quick," he said.

"We were able to create a big offset on tyres, and when I came out of the pit, I was like, 'We have a good chance to fight and to catch the leaders back.'

"But then, of course, with the red flag, everything went back to zero, and everyone then put fresh tyres on, and we were back to base. But then it was good.

"The move on Charles was critical into Turn 1. We were all pushing, the three of us. It was a very high pace, but it was a bit hard to follow, mainly for temperatures.

"We had to manage brake temperatures a lot during the race, so couldn't push as much. But it was still very fun."
